title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
description: Asymptotic notation and recurrences, the main design techniques (divide and conquer, dynamic programming, greedy, randomized), amortized analysis, graph algorithms, spanning trees and NP-completeness.

topics.title: Algorithm Fundamentals and Analysis
topics.summary: An algorithm is a finite sequence of clear instructions that always terminates, and its performance is measured by time and space complexity. Asymptotic notation, recurrences and amortized analysis describe how cost grows with input size and over a sequence of operations.
subtopics: Definition and criteria of an algorithm: input, output, definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness
Time and space complexity; goals of algorithm design
Classification by implementation, design method and design approach
Rate of growth: Big-O, Big-Theta, little-o, little-omega
Recurrences: substitution, recurrence tree, master and iteration methods
Amortized analysis: aggregate, accounting and potential methods

topics.title: Divide and Conquer
topics.summary: Divide and conquer solves a problem by dividing it into sub-problems, solving them recursively and combining their answers. Merge sort and the closest pair of points problem are the worked examples, both running in O(n log n) time.
subtopics: Divide, conquer and combine
Standard algorithms: quicksort, merge sort, closest pair, Strassen, Cooley–Tukey FFT, Karatsuba
How merge sort works and its recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + θ(n)
Applications, advantages and drawbacks of merge sort
Closest pair of points by divide and conquer

topics.title: Dynamic Programming and Memoization
topics.summary: Dynamic programming breaks a problem into overlapping sub-problems and stores their results so they are never recomputed, turning exponential recursion into polynomial time. Memoization (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) are the two ways to store those results.
subtopics: Meaning and characteristics of dynamic programming (Bellman, 1950s)
Recursion versus dynamic programming; drawbacks of recursion
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Top-down and bottom-up approaches
Longest common subsequence, Floyd–Warshall and Bellman–Ford
Memoization: 1-D, 2-D and 3-D; memoization versus tabulation

topics.title: Greedy and Randomized Algorithms
topics.summary: A greedy algorithm takes the best option available at each step and never reverses a choice, so it is simple but not always optimal. A randomized algorithm adds random bits to its logic, as in randomized quicksort (Las Vegas) and Karger's minimum cut (Monte Carlo).
subtopics: Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Advantages and drawbacks of the greedy approach
The greedy algorithm steps; coin change and activity selection
Types of greedy algorithm
Randomized algorithms: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo; amplification
Zero-sum games, randomized quicksort and Karger's minimum cut

topics.title: Graphs, Spanning Trees and NP-Completeness
topics.summary: Graphs model related objects as vertices and edges, are stored as adjacency matrices or lists, and are traversed with breadth-first or depth-first search in O(V + E) time. Minimum spanning trees are found greedily with Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm, while NP-complete problems have no known efficient algorithm.
subtopics: Graph terminology and types of graph
Adjacency matrix and adjacency list
Breadth-first search and depth-first search
Spanning trees and minimum spanning trees
Kruskal's algorithm, union-find and Prim's algorithm
NP, NP-hard and NP-complete; solving NP-complete problems
